{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=autonomous+inquiry+problem+selection+curiosity+information+gain&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Towards a praxis of metacognitive reflection in medical education: a framework of inquiry, adaptive action, and pattern logic.\", \"abstract\": \"Metacognitive reflection is widely recognized as essential for navigating the complexities of clinical practice and medical education. Despite extensive literature emphasizing its importance, a robust framework elucidating its practical application and theory remains a significant gap. The present paper argues that the praxis of metacognitive reflection—how it is enacted and acquired—is best understood and exemplified through the interconnected principles of inquiry, adaptive action, and pattern logic. These three processes offer a novel framework for both explaining the dynamics of metacognitive reflection and cultivating its development in learners and practitioners. By engaging in iterative cycles of inquiry, adapting to evolving contexts, and discerning the logic of underlying complex patterns, individuals can refine their metacognitive capacities, ultimately leading to enhanced clinical practice and learning outcomes, and a more sophisticated understanding of the complex adaptive systems within which healthcare operates. This model has the potential to significantly advance both our theoretical understanding of metacognitive reflection and its practical application in the training and professional development of health professionals.\", \"doi\": \"10.1007/s10459-025-10469-w\", \"pmid\": \"40928621\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13233880\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10469-w\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13233880\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13233880?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Effects of Gen-AI integrated science reading activity on primary school students' intrinsic reading motivation.\", \"abstract\": \"

Introduction

Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) can generate new content such as text, images, audio, and video based on users' needs. This study designed a Gen-AI integrated science reading activity to examine its effects on primary school students' intrinsic reading motivation.

Methods

A mixed research design was adopted with sixth-grade students from a public primary school in central China. Two classes were randomly assigned to an experimental group (Gen-AI integrated reading) and a control group (traditional reading).

Results and discussion

Independent-samples t-tests showed no significant differences between the two groups in intrinsic reading motivation before the experiment. After the intervention, the experimental group showed greater improvement than the control group. ANCOVA results indicated that the Gen-AI integrated science reading approach had significant positive effects on intrinsic reading motivation. Semi-structured interviews further revealed that the approach can satisfy students' autonomy, competence, and relatedness from multiple aspects. In addition, the limitations and future prospects of this study were also discussed.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1865488\", \"pmid\": \"42688913\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13535925\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1865488\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13535925\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13535925?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"AI feedback does not motivate by itself: a motivational-meaning model for university physical education.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951652\", \"pmid\": \"42973821\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13724568\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951652\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13724568\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13724568?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"The future of fundamental science led by generative closed-loop artificial intelligence.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence is approaching the point at which it can complete the scientific cycle, from hypothesis generation to experimental design and validation, within a closed loop that requires little human intervention. Yet, the loop is not fully autonomous: humans still curate data, set hyperparameters, adjudicate interpretability, and decide what counts as a satisfactory explanation. As models scale, they begin to explore regions of hypothesis and solution space that are inaccessible to human reasoning because they are too intricate or alien to our intuitions. Scientists may soon rely on AI strategies they do not fully understand, trusting goals and empirical payoffs rather than derivations. This prospect forces a choice about how much control to relinquish to accelerate discovery while keeping outputs human relevant. The answer cannot be a blanket policy to deploy LLMs or any single paradigm everywhere. It demands principled matching of methods to domains, hybrid causal and neurosymbolic scaffolds around generative models, and governance that preserves plurality and counters recursive bias. Otherwise, recursive training and uncritical reuse risk model collapse in AI and an epistemic collapse in science, as statistical inertia amplifies flaws and narrows the investigation. We argue for graded autonomy in AI-conducted science: systems that can close the loop at machine speed, while remaining anchored to human priorities, verifiable mechanisms, and domain-appropriate forms of understanding.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/frai.2026.1678539\", \"pmid\": \"41755911\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC12932417\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1678539\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12932417\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12932417?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "71faa1c3a42d3cd0e31c4d5585c7f790facf0520fc47114340a4e25b9aa566c3", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_inquiry", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1007/s10459-025-10469-w", "doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1865488", "doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951652", "doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1678539", "pmc:PMC13233880", "pmc:PMC13535925", "pmc:PMC13724568", "pmc:PMC12932417"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10469-w", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13233880", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13233880?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1865488", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13535925", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13535925?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951652", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13724568"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
